stories.title_en: Scamming with Forged Letters from the Education Commissioner to Report Lucky Dreams

paragraphs.en: In the gengzi year, at the Fujian provincial examination, most of the successful candidates from the upper prefectures were men whom Education Commissioner Shen had placed at the top of his list. Everyone praised Commissioner Shen for knowing talent when he saw it.

Early in the twelfth month, when all the juren had departed for the capital, a con man in the provincial city plotted with a calligraphic xiucai from this prefecture. Together they forged letters in Commissioner Shen's name for each graduate, stamped them with a small seal, wrapped and sealed them tightly, and delivered them one by one to the graduates' homes. At each house, the messenger would say: "Master Shen has a letter and has sent me specially. He charged me by word of mouth: your young master is certain of a great triumph next year. The master had a wondrous dream and ordered me to bring you word of it first—but you must guard it closely and let nothing leak. There is also young master so-and-so, whose family lives near yours; if he learned that a special messenger had come, he would say the master favors one and slights another, so a letter of greeting for him is enclosed as well. I merely brought it along—I was not sent for him." And when they came to that other house, they said exactly the same: that they had come specially for him, and all the rest were just brought along. When the families opened the letters, the calligraphy was in a fine, exact hand and the wording subtle and marvelous. Each said the commissioner had received an auspicious dream whose omen fell on that particular man, who was destined to be the great champion. Drawing now on a man's name, now on the meaning of his native place, they contrived a dream for each as the excuse, to foretell his coming glory. I once saw the letter they wrote to the juren Xiong Shaozu. It read: "Fujian abounds in talent, the first in the empire; even the capital and Zhejiang can hardly outdo it. And among all the essays on the Spring and Autumn that I read, none stood above yours. A deep and ample cultivation, issuing in a bold and shining edge—your triumph next spring in the Southern Palace, the metropolitan examination, is certain without divination. On the twenty-second night of the eleventh month, near midnight, I dreamed of a flying bear, a red spring flower raised in its paw, walking through the heart of a red sun, with two gold characters above it, 'Great Champion,' all plain to see. Waking, I pondered it: the sun is Jianyang, your native place; the bear is your surname; the spring flower is the Spring and Autumn, the classic you have made your own. Red is the hue of celebration, and the gold words 'Great Champion' are a manifest omen of luck. Your talent answering my dream is sure proof that in this bright reign you will stand first in the empire. If the great champion is to come from my own school, I shall be too joyful to sleep. I send this man at a gallop to tell you; keep it close and let nothing leak." The Xiong household read it with huge delight and rewarded the messenger with three taels of silver. When he begged for more, they gave him two taels more, saying, "If the great triumph comes next year, we will give you another ten." The letters delivered to the other houses all told lucky dreams to the same effect, and everyone who rewarded him gave three to five taels or more.

The following year, all the silver was gone; they returned south empty-handed. When the new juren gathered for the spring meeting, each recounted Commissioner Shen's letter and the dream within it, clapping their hands and roaring: "A fine spring dream that was, truly!" This trickster was astonishingly clever—cheat people like this, and who wouldn't gladly pay? His takings must have exceeded a hundred taels. I record this briefly to give my reader a laugh.

Note: This crook cheated a newly promoted juren, and the swindle cost him little. For a few taels of silver, he bought four months of joy for the entire household. It's a pity he didn't return; had he run the same game again, people would have gladly paid up. Of all such tricks, this one is the most delightful.

stories.title_en: Posing as Impermanence and Burning a Warrant to Arrest People

paragraphs.en: Changyuan was a place with over a thousand households, a sizable market town. There was a fortune-teller there. His calculations were very precise; his verdicts on life and death, longevity and early demise, were uncannily accurate. Consequently, the old and young, men and women of the countryside, mostly entrusted their destinies to his calculations. For anyone fated to sicken or die within three years, he would ask their name and secretly record it, to verify later. By day he went to the market to tell fortunes; at night he returned to sleep in a Buddhist temple.

A wandering Daoist priest arrived at the temple, his face half-withered, sallow, gaunt, and dark. He paid a respectful call on the fortune-teller and said: "I hear, sir, that your calculations are uncannily accurate. Might I ask you for the names and eight characters of all the old and young in this place who are fated to die this year or to fall ill? In exchange, I offer several proven remedies gathered during my travels." The fortune-teller said, "You do not understand fate; what use are they to you?" The Daoist replied, "I have another use for them." So the fortune-teller copied out every fate he had calculated—all those due for sickness or death that year—and handed the list over. Afterward, the Daoist went begging from door to door. Whenever he met a simple-looking soul, he would announce that he was the Living Impermanence, sent by the underworld court to join its ghost bailiffs in arresting such-and-such persons in the district, with a deadline set for this season. The fools spread the word for him, though most people had yet to hear it. He also secretly wrote a warrant on yellow paper, ending with the two large characters "Underworld Court." In the middle, he itemized, from the fortune-teller's list, the old and young fated to die, writing them in the upper rows; then, having asked the temple for the names of sons and daughters from rich families and of beloved children, he wrote them in the rows just below. At night, he deliberately went to the shrine of the earth god and burned the yellow warrant from the lower end, where there were no names, then stamped out the flames and kept the upper half containing the names. The next day, when people came to pray at the shrine, they saw on the incense burner a half-burned slip of yellow paper with writing on it. Picking it up, they found it full of villagers' names, with "Underworld Court" at the end. Much astonished, they carried the story through the district. Within a month, two of those named actually died, and word went around: "That gaunt Daoist is the Living Impermanence—he must know all about this yellow warrant from the underworld." Everyone whose name was on the warrant came to ask about it; and those not named, fearing their names might have been in the burned section, went to ask too. The Daoist, mumbling and half-hesitant, admitted that he and the ghost bailiffs had burned it. Then those who feared death asked, "Can the underworld warrant be bought off?" The Daoist said, "The underworld is just like a yamen in the mortal world: spend silver and your summons can be arranged away; if they absolutely must arrest you, it can still be put off two or three years. There is nothing silver cannot do." So the sons and daughters of rich houses bribed the Daoist with silver, adding gold and silver spirit money for the dead, and begged him to arrange their exemption; he made off with several dozen taels. Afterwards, most of those named on the warrant did not die—and people actually credited the Daoist's negotiations. What delusion!

Note: Observe: When the underworld arrests a man, what need has it of a paper warrant? If it did issue warrants, why burn one? And if it were burned, why deliberately leave a charred scrap with writing on it for all to see? None of this could possibly be. Look at the episode of the gaunt Impermanence: his duping of the world and swindling of the people is plain to see. Let those who believe in ghostly marvels take this story and wake up.

stories.title_en: Making Fools of Chair-Bearers with Broom Handles

paragraphs.en: From the post station west of the city up to Jianxi is a hundred and twenty li by land, and the regular sedan-chair fare is only one qian six fen. When travelers are scarce on the road, the bearers will knock it down to one qian four or one qian two and still carry you. But once they have coaxed the fare into their hands first, they set the chair down every five li; at the least little slope they put it down again and refuse to go on. All told, you ride two parts of the road and walk one, and every traveler passing through falls into their trap. At examination time, when the candidates head home from the exams, the fare jumps to two qian four, two qian at the very least, and they will not lift the poles until the silver is weighed out in advance. Once the silver is clutched in hand, before they have carried you twenty li they pass you on to bearers bound up the road, shaving your good price down and hiring others at a mere one fen a stage to do the carrying. The men who take over still set you down every five li, forever protesting, "I never got the going rate." The scholars have no choice but to pay more. But scholars seldom travel, and none of them bothers to quarrel over it.

There was a clerk who often traveled this road and had been swindled by chair-bearers time and again. One day he had to go up to the county town again. First he wrote a four-line mocking verse on two slips of paper and wrapped them in square paper; then he took two worn broom handles, cut them to matching lengths, and sealed them up in cotton paper so they looked exactly like two bolts of silk. The next day he set out on the road carrying them himself, and the chair-bearers fought for the job. The clerk said, "I am heading home on urgent business and carry no ready silver. Whoever will take me straight home, we will agree on a fare of two qian, and I will stand you wine and supper tonight and breakfast tomorrow. If you want cash down or to subcontract me, that I cannot do." Two of the bearers agreed to carry him. He tied the two sealed "bolts" to the chair and charged them, "Stow them carefully—mind you don't damage them!" The moment he was seated he added, "At Huiyao Street I must send off an urgent letter to someone. When you get there, whatever you do, don't forget!" Before the afternoon was half spent they reached Huiyao. "Wait here a moment," said the clerk; "I will post the letter and be right back." In fact he slipped away by a side lane and headed home. A meal's time passed and he did not come. The two bearers said, "He is sitting there talking and has lost track of the time. Here are two bolts of silk in our hands—let us just run off home with them. Why wait for him?" The two hurried off and reached home toward evening. One said, "Each of us takes a bolt." The other said, "If one proves better than the other, we even it up between us." They tore open the cotton paper: nothing but two lengths of worn broom handle, wrapped round and round. Each bundle also held a square packet they took for a letter. Opening it, they found a slip inscribed in large characters: "Chair-bearers cheat people every day; today the cheat was mine. But for two broom handles, I narrowly escaped losing two bolts of silk." At home the two cursed loudly: "The sharp! The very prince of sharps!" Chair-bearers from next door heard the noise and came in to ask why they were cursing sharps, and the two told them the whole story. The neighbors roared with laughter, then went out and hung the two broom handles, still half-wrapped and half-showing, on the palisade fence, pasting the two verse slips beside them. Everyone who passed read the verse aloud, looked at the broom handles, and burst out laughing: "This clerk is a master at the game. But you two bearers had no business nursing thieving thoughts. Luckily they were only broom handles, so you can shout your curses in public; had they really been silk, you would be terrified of anyone knowing, and how could the gentleman have come after you for them? The fault is yours—why curse the gentleman?"

Three days later, the clerk returned, saw the verse still pasted on the fence, and therefore asked the neighbors: "Some time ago someone entrusted me with two bolts of silk, which two chair-bearers carried off. Did you happen to hear about it?" The people knew the clerk was making game of the bearers and said, "You need not hunt for the silk—those bearers will not dare show their faces to claim the fare." The clerk laughed heartily and went on his way.

Note: The clerk who swindled a chair ride was no swindler; the two chair-bearers were the crooks. Otherwise, why did the clerk return to ask questions while the bearers dared not show themselves? This is called borrowing the crooks' own tricks to drive out the crooks—quite clever. Still, whenever you travel far and need chair-bearers or porters, hire them through your innkeeper. He knows the laborers' backgrounds, so there is no fear of them running off with your goods.

stories.title_en: A Sham Purchase at the Alley Mouth to Make Off with the Cloth

paragraphs.en: In the main street of Jiancheng there was a side alley that ran through to the back street. At the alley mouth stood a pavilion, with two benches set beside it where people sat and rested, so that it looked just like the entrance to someone's house. Earthen walls flanked both sides of the pavilion, like the gateway path into a residence; only after a turn did the main road ahead come back into view.

One day a crook was sitting in the pavilion when he saw a trader coming with cloth on his back. Recognizing him as no man of this city, he knew the fellow could be gulled. "Buying cloth!" he called. "Bring it into the pavilion, friend." The crook took the cloth and turned it over, picking and choosing, then gathered six bolts in his arms. "I mean to buy three," he said; "let me take six inside to choose among them." With that he turned into the alley and fled out the back street. The cloth seller sat on the bench in the alley for a long while. When one or two passersby came through, suspicion finally stirred, and he followed them in. Rounding the bend of the walled lane, he saw there were no houses on either side; straight ahead, the lane came out on the main road. Only then did he understand that the crook had made off with his cloth. He could only ask the people along the street, "A man came this way just now carrying six bolts of cloth—did any of you see him?" The bystanders said, "This alley sees crowds all day—how would we know who was carrying cloth?" The cloth seller told them how the man had gulled him with a sham purchase. "A swindler has cheated you in broad daylight," the bystanders said. The cloth seller could only curse at the top of his voice and go off filled with regret.

Note: A seller who enters a buyer's home must still follow them all the way inside and verify that their dwelling is genuine and settled before handing over goods. Otherwise, even at a public gateway where households crowd thickly behind it, one must not be quick to trust. Let every merchant take this to heart.
